bibl.title: Revised Estimates for the Number of Human and Bacteria Cells in the Body

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the number of human and bacterial cells in the body, and the provenance of the values the literature repeats for them
span.quote: Reported values in the literature on the number of cells in the body differ by orders of magnitude and are very seldom supported by any measurements or calculations.

span.label: what the two counts actually are when the calculation is documented and its uncertainty derived, and what the widely-cited 10:1 ratio between them rests on
span.quote: By updating the cell counts in the body, we also revisit the 10:1 value that has been so thoroughly repeated as to achieve the status of an established common knowledge fact [4].

span.label: revised estimates with the calculation logic, sources and uncertainty ranges fully documented, replacing the 10:1 ratio with about 1:1 - and the observation that the difference between those two numbers is a definition
span.quote: The aim of this study is to critically revisit former estimates for the number of human and bacterial cells in the human body. We give up-to-date detailed estimates where the calculation logic and sources are fully documented and uncertainty ranges are derived.

span.label: critique
span.quote: By updating the cell counts in the body, we also revisit the 10:1 value that has been so thoroughly repeated as to achieve the status of an established common knowledge fact [4].

span.label: a quantitative claim that propagates through a literature without its warrant, until repetition alone gives it the standing of an established fact
span.quote: Reported values in the literature on the number of cells in the body differ by orders of magnitude and are very seldom supported by any measurements or calculations.

span.label: documented back-of-the-envelope (Fermi) estimation from surveyed sources, with derived uncertainty ranges and an independent mass-balance sanity check
span.term: documented back-of-the-envelope (Fermi) estimation from surveyed sources, with derived uncertainty ranges and an independent mass-balance sanity check
span.quote: Doing so, we repeat and reflect on the assumptions in previous back-of-the-envelope calculations, also known as Fermi problems. We find such estimates as effective sanity checks and a way to improve our quantitative understanding in biology.

span.label: the B/H ratio is a quotient whose numerator is fixed but whose denominator depends on whether enucleated cells are counted; because red blood cells dominate the human count, that single definitional choice moves the published value by a factor of ten
span.quote: This is because the dominant population of non-nucleated red blood cells is not included in the calculation.

span.label: a value stated without a primary reference is re-cited by papers that cite the re-citation, so the chain grows while the evidence at its root stays a single order-of-magnitude calculation, and the value acquires standing from the citation count rather than from measurement
span.quote: Reported values in the literature on the number of cells in the body differ by orders of magnitude and are very seldom supported by any measurements or calculations.

span.label: multiplying a measured bacterial concentration by organ volume makes the colon exceed every other site by orders of magnitude, which collapses a body-wide estimation problem into a single-organ one
span.quote: Table 1 reveals that the bacterial content of the colon exceeds all other organs by at least two orders of magnitude. Importantly, within the alimentary tract, the colon is the only substantial contributor to the total bacterial population, while the stomach and small intestine make negligible contributions.

span.label: the human-cell literature the estimate is built from used cohorts of exclusively or mostly men, so the analysis begins with adult men and generalises outward
span.quote: A major part of the available literature used in the derivation of human cell numbers was based on cohorts of exclusively or mostly men

span.label: the headline ratio is contingent on a definitional choice the authors make explicitly and defend as plausible either way - a reader who counts only nucleated cells gets 10:1 from the same data
span.quote: The issue of whether cells without a nucleus should be included or discarded in the calculation of the number of human cells, and thus the B/ H ratio, seems to be a question of definition.

span.label: the whole subject is a standardised 70 kg reference man taken from an external report, not a measured population
span.quote: For our analysis, we used the definition of the standard reference man as given in the literature [6] as: "Reference Man is defined as being between 20–30 years of age, weighing 70 kg, is 170 cm in height.”

span.label: per-organ bacterial numbers are rounded up to an order-of-magnitude upper bound, so the non-colon contributions are ceilings rather than estimates
span.quote: The estimates are based on multiplying measured concentrations of bacteria by the volume of each organ [9,10]. Values are rounded up to give an order of magnitude upper bound.

span.label: `bacteria` is used operationally for all microbial cells, on the grounds that they outnumber eukaryotes and archaea - so the count is a microbial count under a bacterial name
span.quote: Bacteria overwhelmingly outnumber eukaryotes and archaea in the human microbiome by 2–3 orders of magnitude [7,8]. We therefore sometimes operationally refer to the microbial cells in the human body as bacteria.

span.label: Fermi estimation, carried from physics pedagogy into quantitative cell biology and defended there as a sanity check rather than as a placeholder for measurement
span.quote: Doing so, we repeat and reflect on the assumptions in previous back-of-the-envelope calculations, also known as Fermi problems. We find such estimates as effective sanity checks and a way to improve our quantitative understanding in biology.

span.label: mass balance, carried from chemistry and physiology to audit a cell COUNT by checking the total mass those cells would have to have
span.quote: It is prudent in making such estimates to approach the analysis from different angles. In that spirit, we now ask does the cumulative mass of the cells counted fall within the expected range for a reference adult?

span.label: an independent mass-centred calculation, asking whether the cumulative mass of the cells counted falls within the expected mass of a reference adult
span.note: eliminates: a cell count that is internally consistent and cannot be reconciled with the mass of the body it is a count of · outcome: held
span.quote: It is prudent in making such estimates to approach the analysis from different angles. In that spirit, we now ask does the cumulative mass of the cells counted fall within the expected range for a reference adult?

span.label: rounding every non-colon organ estimate UP, so that the colon's dominance is argued against the most generous possible rivals
span.note: eliminates: the colon's dominance being an artefact of generous rounding in its favour - every rival organ is rounded UP instead · outcome: held
span.quote: The estimates are based on multiplying measured concentrations of bacteria by the volume of each organ [9,10]. Values are rounded up to give an order of magnitude upper bound.

span.label: a sensitivity check on the definitional choice the headline ratio rests on: recomputing it counting only nucleated human cells
span.note: eliminates: a headline ratio that exists only under one definitional choice about what counts as a human cell · outcome: failed
span.quote: This is because the dominant population of non-nucleated red blood cells is not included in the calculation.

span.label: B/H value
span.quote: This B/H value of about 1:1 (with the associated uncertainty range) should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values that are stated in the literature until more accurate measurements become available.

span.label: back-of-the-envelope
span.quote: Doing so, we repeat and reflect on the assumptions in previous back-of-the-envelope calculations, also known as Fermi problems. We find such estimates as effective sanity checks and a way to improve our quantitative understanding in biology.

span.label: Fermi problems
span.quote: Doing so, we repeat and reflect on the assumptions in previous back-of-the-envelope calculations, also known as Fermi problems. We find such estimates as effective sanity checks and a way to improve our quantitative understanding in biology.

span.label: uncertainty ranges
span.quote: The aim of this study is to critically revisit former estimates for the number of human and bacterial cells in the human body. We give up-to-date detailed estimates where the calculation logic and sources are fully documented and uncertainty ranges are derived.

span.label: reference man
span.quote: For our analysis, we used the definition of the standard reference man as given in the literature [6] as: "Reference Man is defined as being between 20–30 years of age, weighing 70 kg, is 170 cm in height.”

span.label: red blood cells
span.quote: We view red blood cells as bona fide cells, as their name suggests. But it is also plausible to choose not to include them as some may think of them as “bags full of hemoglobin.”

span.label: platelets
span.quote: Inclusion of platelets in the count, which corresponds to their inclusion in previous counts, is also potentially disputable but has only a minor quantitative effect.

span.label: hematopoietic lineage
span.quote: The striking dominance of the hematopoietic lineage in the cell count (90% of the total) is counterintuitive given the composition of the body by mass.

span.label: colon
span.quote: Table 1 reveals that the bacterial content of the colon exceeds all other organs by at least two orders of magnitude. Importantly, within the alimentary tract, the colon is the only substantial contributor to the total bacterial population, while the stomach and small intestine make negligible contributions.

span.label: alimentary tract
span.quote: Table 1 reveals that the bacterial content of the colon exceeds all other organs by at least two orders of magnitude. Importantly, within the alimentary tract, the colon is the only substantial contributor to the total bacterial population, while the stomach and small intestine make negligible contributions.

span.label: total cell mass
span.quote: In contrast, 75% of total cell mass is composed of two cell types, fat cells (adipocytes) and muscle cells (myocytes), both large cells (usually >10,000 μm3 by volume)

span.quote: In contrast, 75% of total cell mass is composed of two cell types, fat cells (adipocytes) and muscle cells (myocytes), both large cells (usually >10,000 μm3 by volume)

span.quote: In contrast, 75% of total cell mass is composed of two cell types, fat cells (adipocytes) and muscle cells (myocytes), both large cells (usually >10,000 μm3 by volume)

span.label: order of magnitude upper bound
span.quote: The estimates are based on multiplying measured concentrations of bacteria by the volume of each organ [9,10]. Values are rounded up to give an order of magnitude upper bound.

span.label: bacteria-to-human-cell ratio - counting ALL human cells, including the enucleated red blood cells and platelets that dominate the count: about 1:1
span.quote: This B/H value of about 1:1 (with the associated uncertainty range) should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values that are stated in the literature until more accurate measurements become available.

span.label: bacteria-to-human-cell ratio - counting only NUCLEATED human cells, which excludes the dominant non-nucleated red-blood-cell population and so returns the larger, older ratio. The paper states its value in a sentence the extraction damaged
span.quote: This is because the dominant population of non-nucleated red blood cells is not included in the calculation.

span.label: contradicts → the widely-repeated 10:1 ratio of bacterial to human cells in the body
span.quote: This B/H value of about 1:1 (with the associated uncertainty range) should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values that are stated in the literature until more accurate measurements become available.

span.label: critiques → order-of-magnitude statements of human and bacterial cell number that give no primary reference and no uncertainty estimate
span.quote: Reported values in the literature on the number of cells in the body differ by orders of magnitude and are very seldom supported by any measurements or calculations.

span.label: builds-on → the letter to Microbe that criticised the 10:1 ratio without supplying an alternative estimate or an uncertainty range
span.quote: This ratio was criticized recently in a letter to the journal Microbe [5], but an alternative detailed estimate that will give concrete values and estimate the uncertainty range is needed.

span.label: extends → the Report of the Task Group on Reference Man, whose standardised body is adopted as the subject of the calculation
span.quote: For our analysis, we used the definition of the standard reference man as given in the literature [6] as: "Reference Man is defined as being between 20–30 years of age, weighing 70 kg, is 170 cm in height.”

span.label: cell count and cell mass rank the body's tissues in almost opposite orders - 90% of cells are hematopoietic, 75% of mass is fat and muscle
span.term: cell count and cell mass rank the body's tissues in almost opposite orders - 90% of cells are hematopoietic, 75% of mass is fat and muscle
span.quote: A striking outcome of this juxtaposition is the evident discordance between contributors to total cell mass and to cell number.
